newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche to show no mercy for fund failings.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche to show no mercy for fund failings.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank will not spare anyone found to have made mistakes at its troubled British fund management business Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, British newspapers said on Sunday.

A number of reports said there was pressure at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Deutsche's London-based investment banking arm, to identify who should be held responsible for failing to spot irregularities in three of its funds, which surfaced last week.
Several papers named Glynn Owen, MGAM's chief European investment officer, and Keith Percy, its chief executive, as those likely to face criticism if failings are exposed.

The Independent on Sunday said the role of Mike Wheatley, compliance director for the fund management business, was also under scrutiny. But Michael Dobson, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's chief executive and a member of the Deutsche board, is not considered to be in the firing line over the episode.

The Sunday Times said an official at British investments watchdog the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) had suggested Deutsche would announce at least one resignation before it had completed its own investigation.
"Deutsche is making so much noise, I think they will take the knives out first," it quoted the IMRO official as saying.
Senior Deutsche officials have already announced an overhaul of supervision at MGAM. The Sunday Times said this review of controls in the unit-trust business will be overseen by Dobson.
Deutsche Bank, which stepped in to rescue the funds, is considering putting MGAM under Frankfurt's direct control.

Trading in the three funds, which total around 1.4 billion pounds ($2.2 billion) and were held by around 90,000 retail investors, was temporarily suspended last week and Peter Young, manager of two of them, suspended. Later his assets were also frozen.

A probe into his management of two of the funds, which held a high proportion of unlisted, speculative high-technology stock, is underway, with MGAM and IMRO together carrying out a detailed dissection of the trading history of the three funds,

A Deutsche Morgan Grenfell spokesman confirmed reports that accounting firm Ernst & Young had been appointed "as an independent auditor to review the portfolios" while IMRO's Judy Delaforce told Reuters it had appointed its own firm.

"They will be looking at the question of whether compensation is due, the basis of the calculation and the amount. Morgan Grenfell are writing to their investors today to inform them of that," she said.

"It is a long process and may take some months. But it is happening, it is being looked at and people will not lose out because some of the unquoted shares may have been incorrectly priced," she added.

Delaforce said the accountants would, where necessary, revalue the shares. This would enable them to establish whether compensation is due for any deals placed for the period from when shares with suspected irregularities were first brought into the fund up to the point where the funds were suspended.

Trading in the funds resumed after a 180 million pound cash injection by Deutsche Bank to ensure sufficient liquidity in the funds to match any flight from them. By Friday worried investors had withdrawn around 200 million pounds, with some industry sources prediciting further fall-out in the coming weeks.

Delaforce could not confirm whether General Accident and the Royal Bank of Scotland, which acted as trustees for the funds, would be investigated. The Sunday Telegraph said MGAM was itself considering suing advisers to the funds to recover losses.
Problems came to light when it was discovered Young had exceeded the maximum 10 percent limit on holdings of unlisted stocks and he was ordered to reduce these to five percent.
Rather than reduce them, however, Young is alleged by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell to have set up more unlisted holding companies in which to place some of the original shares. ($1=.6385 Pound)
